children.text: The Philippines' northernmost province, Batanes is a cluster of remote islands closer to Taiwan than to the rest of the country, where rolling grass hills sweep endlessly toward the sea and Ivatan stone houses built to withstand typhoons complete the scene. It's hard to reach and expensive, but many consider it the most exotic and peaceful destination in the Philippines.
Batanes is the Philippines' northernmost province, made up of 10 islands scattered across the Bashi Channel, about
160 km
from the northern coast of mainland Luzon and about
190 km

from the southern tip of Taiwan. Only three islands are inhabited: Batan, home to the capital Basco; Sabtang, where traditional villages remain well preserved; and Itbayat, the largest island. With a population of roughly 18,000, it is one of the smallest provinces in the Philippines.

Batanes is often called "the Philippines that doesn't feel like the Philippines." Instead of palm-lined beaches, it has green pastures rolling gently down toward the sea, black rocky coasts where waves crash, and hills where cattle graze — scenery that brings Scotland or New Zealand to mind. Since typhoons pass through several times a year, the native Ivatan people have long built stone houses with walls nearly
1 m
thick, made of limestone and coral stone and topped with thick cogon-grass roofs. In the village of Chavayan on Sabtang Island, rows of these traditional stone houses still line the lanes today.

The people here are also famous for their honesty. The unstaffed "Honesty Coffee Shop" in Ivana, where customers calculate their own bill and leave the money themselves, has become a symbol of Batanes, and the crime rate is so low that the streets feel safe even at night.

With essentially only one flight route, airfare is expensive, and both planes and boats are frequently canceled depending on the weather, making this a demanding destination. For that reason, Batanes isn't a quick stopover but more of a slow-travel destination, best enjoyed over at least
3 nights and 4 days
, touring the islands leisurely by bicycle or tricycle. For travelers drawn to scenic photography, quiet rest, and traditional culture, it's a place worth visiting at least once in a lifetime.
The Ivatan originally lived near cliff fortresses called "ijang." On
, an expedition sent by the Spanish governor José Basco y Vargas formally annexed the islands, and the capital took his name (Basco); from
, residents moved down to the coastal villages where they live today. The whole province is a protected area, designated the "Batanes Protected Landscape and Seascape" in
, and it has been on UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List since
. Mount Iraya, rising
above sea level in northern Batan Island, last erupted in
but is still managed as an active volcano.

blocks.title: Vayang Rolling Hills and Naidi Hill lighthouse

children.text: Vayang Rolling Hills, north of Basco, is Batanes' signature view, where the grassland rolls like waves and drops into the sea. The white lighthouse on Naidi Hill, close to downtown Basco, is a sunset hotspot. Basco Lighthouse, completed in
, is a six-story lighthouse about
tall, and from its fifth-floor observation deck you can see Mount Iraya, Sabtang Island to the south, and Itbayat Island to the north. It is about
1.2 km
from Basco Port, so you can even walk up.

A vast communal pasture in Mahatao, nicknamed "Marlboro Country" for its resemblance to the ranch in the old cigarette ads. Grazing cattle, Mount Iraya in the distance, and the Pacific cliffs all fit into one frame here.
From Radiwan Port in Ivana, a traditional boat called a faluwa takes about
30–45 minutes
to cross over to the Ivatan stone-house villages of Savidug and Chavayan. In Chavayan, you can try on the vakul, the traditional headgear worn by local women, for photos.

At Morong Beach on Sabtang Island stands a massive natural rock arch rising from the sea. It's often used as a lunch spot on Sabtang tours, and eating an Ivatan-style packed lunch on the beach here is a special experience.
On the coast east of Basco, round boulders spewed out by Mount Iraya cover the beach instead of sand. The sound of waves rolling the boulders is striking, and it's a favorite spot for sunrise.

blocks.title: Honesty Coffee Shop and House of Dakay in Ivana

children.text: At the Honesty Coffee Shop, run on an unstaffed honor system, buy coffee and snacks, then write down your purchase in the ledger and pay for it yourself. The nearby House of Dakay is a stone house built in
, famous for surviving the great earthquake of
. The Honesty Coffee Shop opened in
and is close to Ivana Port, where the boats to Sabtang depart.
Saint Carlos Borromeo Church in Mahatao was first built in
and rebuilt to its present form in
; this stone church was declared a National Cultural Treasure in
. Saint Joseph Church in Ivana retains a stone church built in
and a fortress-like bell tower raised in
. Mount Carmel Chapel (Tukon Church) on Tukon Hill in Basco is a chapel newly built in
in the Ivatan stone-house style, with outstanding views over Mount Iraya and the sea.

Renting a bicycle in Basco and riding along the coastal roads is the most authentically Batanes way to see the island. Traffic is light and the roads are well paved, but the hills are steep enough that an electric bike is worth considering.

Itbayat is the largest island in Batanes, but most of its coast is high cliffs, so there are almost no sandy beaches. Boats are operated by M/B Ocean Spirit and Itransa, and there are also light aircraft, but with only a few seats. If a boat is canceled, you may be stuck for a day or more, so don't make the trip right before your flight to Clark.
This is practically the only realistic way to get there. PAL Express's Manila–Basco route ended in
October 2025
, so a Clark–Basco (BSO) flight now operates daily, with a flight time of about
1 hour 30 minutes
. One-way fares vary widely, from around
in sale periods to
or more in peak season, so booking several months ahead is essential. Check the latest flight information.
From Manila, take a Genesis bus company P2P bus to Clark International Airport. Buses depart NAIA Terminal 3 every hour at
one way (about
from Trinoma and Cubao), also leave from PITX, and take about
2–3 hours
. Flights to Basco leave around
, so to avoid Manila's morning traffic it's safest to stay the night before in
Clark
or Angeles.
Another route promoted by the provincial tourism office is Sky Pasada's Tuguegarao–Basco flight, which takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes

. It's a 19-seat L-410 small aircraft, so seats are limited and sell out early, and baggage weight limits are strict, so check the conditions when booking. Flights from Laoag and Binalonan (Pangasinan), and routes by other small airlines such as Fliteline Airways and Northsky Air, repeatedly stop and resume operation, so check whether they are currently running.

There is essentially no regular passenger ferry from mainland Luzon to Batanes, only irregular cargo ships, which are not recommended for travelers. Inter-island travel uses the traditional faluwa boat. Radiwan Port on Batan Island to Sabtang Island takes about
30–45 minutes
, and Basco to Itbayat about
3–4 hours
, with cancellations on rough-sea days. Small planes also fly to Itbayat from Basco at times.
Basco Airport is right next to town, so it's
5–10 minutes
by tricycle to your lodging. For sightseeing around the island, choose from tricycle tours driven by a driver-guide (per tricycle, about
for the northern route and about
for the southern route), van tours, or bicycle, e-bike and scooter rentals. On Sabtang Island, too, you take a tricycle tour from the port (about
per tricycle).
Many tricycles in Batanes have roofs modeled on traditional Ivatan houses, and in
August 2026

a provincial ordinance gave them the official name "Vahaycycle." Tours are usually booked the day before through your lodging or the Basco tricycle association (BATODA), and the trip from Basco to Ivana Port, where boats to Sabtang depart, takes about
30–45 minutes
and costs about
one way.
The best time is from
March
to
June
. Winds and waves die down, so flights and the Sabtang faluwa run relatively reliably, the grasslands are green, and the skies are clear.
April–May
in particular is the peak season for Batanes travel, with flights and lodging filling quickly. March–April is the driest stretch of the year.
March–May
is the season when Ivatan fishermen catch mahi-mahi (arayu) using flying fish as bait, and in
early to mid-March
a ceremony opening the fishing season is held at places such as the Diura fishing village in Mahatao. Also, around
June 26
, Batanes Day (commemorating its founding in 1783), the province-wide "Bunung Festival" is held, with processions in traditional costume and the sharing of "bunung," food wrapped in kabaya leaves.
From
July
to
October

is typhoon season. Batanes is one of the places typhoons pass through most often in the Philippines, and when one hits, flights can be grounded for days, stranding travelers on the island. If traveling during this period, build 2–3 spare days into your itinerary.
From
November
to
February
, the strong northeast monsoon blows, so average January temperatures fall to around
in the morning and
in the afternoon, and can drop below

when cold air arrives. It rains about half of each month and the sea is rough, so boats to Sabtang and Itbayat are often canceled. You can feel rare chilly weather by Philippine standards, but rain and strong winds put many limits on outdoor sightseeing. Holy Week and the
April–May
school-vacation season bring the most domestic travelers, so for these periods it's safest to book flights and lodging at least three months ahead.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Most lodging is clustered in the capital, Basco, with family-run guesthouses priced around

per night. For something more special, Fundacion Pacita — a boutique lodge converted from the old studio of Filipino painter Pacita Abad — is well known; it sits on a hilltop overlooking the sea with a wonderful view, though rates are higher and rooms fill up early. With few rooms available on the island, secure your lodging along with your flight, especially in peak season.

Ivatan food is simple but distinctive. Signature dishes include uvod (banana pith minced and stir-fried with meat), lunis (pork salted and slow-cooked in oil), dibang (dried flying fish), and various seaweed and seafood dishes. Fresh lobster and fish are also available at reasonable prices. There are few large restaurants on the island, so meals are typically at your lodging or a small home-style eatery, and lunch during tours often comes as an Ivatan packed lunch wrapped in banana leaf. The coconut crab is an endangered species and protected, so even if it appears on a menu, it's best not to order it.
In the Department of Tourism (DOT)-accredited accommodation list published by the provincial tourism office (as of
January 2025

), the only hotel-class property is Fundacion Pacita; the rest are homestay-type inns and lodges such as Pension Ivatan and Casa Feliciano in Basco, and small properties such as Panayanan Pension House in Malakdang, Sabtang. Pension Ivatan also runs an Ivatan home-cooking restaurant, and the pizzeria Casa Napoli is popular with travelers too. Ivatan dishes worth trying include "vunes," dried young taro stems cooked with fish or meat, "lataven," raw fish dressed with ginger, onion and calamansi, and yellow sticky rice cooked with turmeric. In
March–May
, flying fish and mahi-mahi (arayu) are at their freshest.
From
, all visitors must pre-register on the provincial government's
visitor registration portal
and pay
per person (ecotourism tax
+ visitor ID

). You enter your ID, a selfie, your accommodation and a DOT-accredited tour operator; after approval, show the QR code you receive by email at the airport or port to get a visitor ID card that works as an entry pass to tourist sites. Children under 12 are exempt from the ecotourism tax, and seniors and persons with disabilities get a 20% discount. Be sure to check the latest announcements before departure.
The island has a few ATMs, but they often break down or run out of cash. Bring most of your cash for the trip from Manila.
Build in a spare 1–2 days between your return flight and any connecting international flight, in case of flight cancellations.
The faluwa to Sabtang is meant to depart in the calm early morning and return by around noon. Confirm with your lodging or guide the night before whether it's sailing.
The wind is strong and the weather changes fast. Bring a light windbreaker, long sleeves, and a small umbrella; from
November to February
a light coat is also needed.
Phone signal is generally good in downtown Basco but weak on the sea cliffs and in parts of Sabtang.
Restaurants close early and menus are limited, so it's convenient to arrange dinner with your lodging in advance.
The best light for photos is within
2 hours
of sunrise and the
2 hours
before sunset. Midday sun is harsh and there's little shade.
In
March 2025

, the DOT Regional Office 2 advised that "Batanes is not a DIY destination" and recommended traveling with accredited tour operators and guides. It isn't prohibited, but with no public transportation between attractions, it's more efficient to arrange a driver-guide tricycle tour through your lodging.
A list of accredited lodgings, restaurants, tour operators and drivers, plus the event schedule, is available on the
official website
of the Batanes Provincial Heritage and Tourism Office.
During typhoon season (
July–October
), you could be stranded on the island for days. Get travel insurance and set aside an emergency budget.
Most cliffside viewpoints have no railing. Don't get close to the edge on windy days.
The cattle and goats on the grassland belong to local residents. Don't cross pasture fences, and don't startle the animals.
The stone houses are still lived in by residents. Always ask permission before looking inside or taking photos.
Unstaffed honor-system shops like the Honesty Coffee Shop are part of Batanes's culture of trust. Make sure not to skip paying.
Even without a typhoon, the southwest monsoon (habagat) alone can cause cancellations to continue. Basco Airport's runway is short at
and flights don't operate when winds exceed safety limits; in
August 2025
more than 60 passengers were stranded for nearly
1 week
, and in
August 2026
about 100 tourists and residents had to wait for an air force transport plane after rain and wind that lasted more than
2 weeks
The biggest variable in a Batanes trip is the weather. Plan generously, assuming flights and boats can be canceled at any time.
A remote island reached overland via Santa Ana and Tuguegarao in Cagayan province, completing a northern Luzon frontier trip together with Batanes.
The northernmost beach resort on Luzon, which can be combined with the Laoag–Basco small aircraft (Sky Pasada).
A coastal wind farm that pairs well with a visit to Pagudpud.
A snow-white, sculpture-like rock formation on the northern Ilocos coast.
A good stop if you take the Tuguegarao–Basco small plane: a limestone cave about
24 km
from downtown Tuguegarao (
40 minutes–1 hour
by tricycle). It's where fossils of the early human Homo luzonensis were found.
